title: Sexual Dysfunction in Multiple Sclerosis: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Clinical, Radiological, and Psychological Correlates
content: Background/Objectives: Sexual dysfunction is a common but underrecognized complication of multiple sclerosis (MS). This study investigated the prevalence, clinical characteristics, and independent clinical and radiological factors associated with sexual dysfunction in people with MS. Methods: This single-center cross-sectional study included 161 patients with MS. Neurological disability, depressive symptoms, urinary dysfunction, and MS-related sexual symptoms were assessed using the Expanded Disability Status Scale, Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire–Short Form (ICIQ-SF), and Multiple Sclerosis Intimacy and Sexuality Questionnaire-19 (MSISQ-19), respectively. Sexual dysfunction was defined according to validated sex-specific cut-off values on the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) and the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF). Independent associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Results: Sexual dysfunction was identified in 119 of 161 patients (73.9%). Patients with sexual dysfunction had greater neurological disability, more frequent spinal cord lesions, and more severe urinary symptoms than those without sexual dysfunction. In multivariable analysis, depressive symptom severity (adjusted OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.01–1.12; p = 0.027) and EDSS score (adjusted OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.24–2.06; p < 0.001) remained independently associated with sexual dysfunction . Conclusions: Sexual dysfunction is highly prevalent in people with MS. Although neurological disability remains an important independent correlate, depressive symptom severity also contributes independently, underscoring the need for routine assessment of both neurological and psychological factors as part of comprehensive MS care.
